q-135308.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.3 & 0.8 \\ 0.7 & 0.2\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}0.1 \\ 0.9\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the stochastic matrix $P$ and vector $q$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true?

I. $q$ is a stochastic vector

II. $Pq=q$

III. $q$ is a steady-state vector of $P$
q-135308.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that $Pq=q.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $q$ is a stochastic vector since its entries are non-negative and add up to $1.$

- Statement II is false. Note that

$$
Pq=[\begin{aligned}0.3 & 0.8 \\ 0.7 & 0.2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.1 \\ 0.9\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.03+0.72 \\ 0.07+0.18\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.75 \\ 0.25\end{aligned}]\ne q.
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $Pq\ne q,$ it is not a steady-state vector of $P.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

q-110242.name: Question 6
q-110242.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.4 & 0.1 \\ 0.6 & 0.9\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P,$ what is the value of $a-b?$
q-110242.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.4 & 0.1 \\ 0.6 & 0.9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.1 \\ 0.6 & -0.1\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0.6 & -0.1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{6}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{7}{6}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{6}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{7} \\ \frac{6}{7}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a-b=\frac{1}{7}-\frac{6}{7}=-\frac{5}{7}.$

q-135408.name: Question 7
q-135408.problem:
There are two groups of people In a small town: those who travel to work by car and those who travel by train. Every year a study is done in which people are asked about their preference between using trains versus cars. The table below shows the results of this study.
From:
Car Train
To: Car $0.35$ $0.25$
Train $0.65$ $0.75$
It's found that $65%$ of people who currently travel by car will switch to train next year, while $25%$ of people who currently travel by train will switch to their car next year. Assuming that the town has $90\,000$ people that travel to work by train or car, and the given probabilities remain constant over many years, how many people will eventually use the train to travel to work?
q-135408.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.35 & 0.25 \\ 0.65 & 0.75\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $P$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.35 & 0.25 \\ 0.65 & 0.75\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.65 & 0.25 \\ 0.65 & -0.25\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.65 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 0.65 & -0.25 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.65 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=\frac{5}{13}{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{13}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{13}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{18}{13}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{13}{18}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{18} \\ \frac{13}{18}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, $\frac{13}{18}$ of the people will eventually use the train to travel. Therefore, the number of people who will eventually use the train is

$$
\frac{13}{18}\cdot 90\,000=65\,000.
$$

Question 7
?

There are two groups of people In a small town: those who travel to work by car and those who travel by train. Every year a study is done in which people are asked about their preference between using trains versus cars. The table below shows the results of this study.

From:
Car Train
To: Car 0.35 0.25
Train 0.65 0.75

It's found that 65% of people who currently travel by car will switch to train next year, while 25% of people who currently travel by train will switch to their car next year.

Assuming that the town has 90000 people that travel to work by train or car, and the given probabilities remain constant over many years, how many people will eventually use the train to travel to work?

a
65000
b
64000
c
63000
d
62000
e
60000
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix P=[0.350.250.650.75].

Notice that P contains only positive entries. So, the matrix P is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of P, and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix P is a stochastic vector q such that

Pq=q⟹(P−I)q=0.

Computing P−I, we get

P−I=[0.350.250.650.75]−[1001]=[−0.650.250.65−0.25].

So, the matrix equation (P−I)q=0 is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M, which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

M=[−0.650.2500.65−0.250]R2:=R2+R1∼[−0.650.250000]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=513x2.

Hence, the general solution is [513x2x2],x2∈R.

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to 1. Therefore, we have 513x2+x2=11813x2=1x2=1318.

Therefore, q=[5181318].

So, 1318 of the people will eventually use the train to travel. Therefore, the number of people who will eventually use the train is 1318⋅90000=65000.

q-135325.name: Question 8
q-135325.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.3 \\ 1 & 0.7\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P,$ what is the value of $a-b?$
q-135325.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.3 \\ 1 & 0.7\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0.3 \\ 1 & -0.3\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 1 & -0.3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+0.3{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 10{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2} & =0 \\ {x}_{1} & =\frac{3}{10}{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{10}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{10}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{13}{10}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{10}{13}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{13} \\ \frac{10}{13}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a-b=\frac{3}{13}-\frac{10}{13}=-\frac{7}{13}.$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

$$

$$

q-111172.name: Question 10
q-111172.problem:
The migration table below describes the movement of the population between cities and suburbs every year in a certain state.
From:
Cities Suburbs
To: Cities $0.8$ $0.7$
Suburbs $0.2$ $0.3$
That is, $20%$ of those living in cities move to the suburbs each year, and $70%$ of those living in suburbs move to the cities. Assuming that the population of the state is $9$ million and remains constant, how many people would eventually live in cities if the given probabilities remain constant over many years?
q-111172.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.8 & 0.7 \\ 0.2 & 0.3\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $P$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.8 & 0.7 \\ 0.2 & 0.3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 0.7 \\ 0.2 & -0.7\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 0.7 & 0 \\ 0.2 & -0.7 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 0.7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{7}{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{2}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{9}{2}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{9} \\ \frac{2}{9}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, after many years, $\frac{7}{9}$ of the $9$ million population will live in cities. Therefore, the total number of people living in cities after many years will be

$$
\frac{7}{9}\cdot 9\,\text{million}=7\,\text{million}.
$$

q-135349.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0.4 & 0.5 \\ 0.6 & 0.1 & 0.3 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & 0.2\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P$ shown above, what is the value of $a+b-c?$
q-135349.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0.4 & 0.5 \\ 0.6 & 0.1 & 0.3 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & 0.2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.9 & 0.4 & 0.5 \\ 0.6 & -0.9 & 0.3 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & -0.8\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.9 & 0.4 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0.6 & -0.9 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & -0.8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=10{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & 4 & 5 & 0 \\ 6 & -9 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 5 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 & -8 & 0 \\ 6 & -9 & 3 & 0 \\ -9 & 4 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -19 & 19 & 0 \\ 0 & 19 & -19 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -19 & 19 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}={x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{3}-8{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}={x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 3{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b-c=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

q-135344.name: Question 13
q-135344.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.4 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0.3 & 0.2 & 0.65 \\ 0.3 & 0.6 & 0.25\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P$ shown above, what is the value of $a+b-c?$
q-135344.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.4 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0.3 & 0.2 & 0.65 \\ 0.3 & 0.6 & 0.25\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0.3 & -0.8 & 0.65 \\ 0.3 & 0.6 & -0.75\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.2 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0.3 & -0.8 & 0.65 & 0 \\ 0.3 & 0.6 & -0.75 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=5{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 3 & -8 & 6.5 & 0 \\ 3 & 6 & -7.5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & -7 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}={x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-3{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}+0.5{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ \frac{5}{2}{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ \frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b-c=\frac{1}{5}+\frac{2}{5}-\frac{2}{5}=\frac{1}{5}.
$$

q-141035.name: Question 14
q-141035.problem:
A study shows how the sports preferences of young people in a certain community vary from year to year. The following table shows the results of this study.
From:
Baseball Basketball Football
To: Baseball $0.8$ $0.2$ $0$
Basketball $0.1$ $0.6$ $0.2$
Football $0.1$ $0.2$ $0.8$
For example, $10%$ of people who used to prefer baseball now prefer football. Given that $1\,260$ young people were interviewed for the study and that the probabilities listed remain constant for many years, how many of those people will eventually prefer baseball?
q-141035.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.8 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.1 & 0.6 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.8\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix ${P}^{2}$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. 
As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.8 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.1 & 0.6 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.8\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.1 & -0.4 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & -0.2\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.1 & -0.4 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & -0.2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=-5{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -4 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}+0{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}+\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ \frac{7}{3}{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{3}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{7} \\ \frac{2}{7} \\ \frac{3}{7}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, after many years, $\frac{2}{7}$ of the people will prefer baseball. Therefore, the number of people who will prefer baseball is

$$
\frac{2}{7}\cdot 1\,260=360\,\text{people}.
$$

Question 14
?

A study shows how the sports preferences of young people in a certain community vary from year to year. The following table shows the results of this study.

From:
Baseball Basketball Football
To: Baseball 0.8 0.2 0
Basketball 0.1 0.6 0.2
Football 0.1 0.2 0.8

For example, 10% of people who used to prefer baseball now prefer football.

Given that 1260 young people were interviewed for the study and that the probabilities listed remain constant for many years, how many of those people will eventually prefer baseball?

a
180
b
360
c
630
d
540
e
720
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix

P=[0.80.200.10.60.20.10.20.8].

Notice that the matrix P2 contains only positive entries. So, the matrix P is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the steady-state vector of P, and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix P is a stochastic vector q such that

Pq=q⟹(P−I)q=0.

Computing P−I, we get

P−I=[0.80.200.10.60.20.10.20.8]−[100010001]=[−0.20.200.1−0.40.20.10.2−0.2].

The matrix equation (P−I)q=0 is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M, which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

M=[−0.20.200.1−0.40.20.10.2−0.2]R1:=−5R1R2:=10R2R3:=10R3∼[1−1001−42012−20]R2:=R2+(−1)R1R3:=R3+(−1)R1∼[1−1000−32003−20]R3:=R3+R2∼[1−1000−3200000]

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the 1st and 2nd). Thus, x3 is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain x2=23x3. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

x1−23x3+0x3=0⟹x1=23x3.

Hence, the general solution is [23x323x3x3],x3∈R.

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to 1. Therefore, we have

23x3+23x3+x3=173x3=1x3=37.

Therefore,

q=[272737].

So, after many years, 27 of the people will prefer baseball. Therefore, the number of people who will prefer baseball is 27⋅1260=360people.

q-141024.name: Question 15
q-141024.problem:
A study conducted on $3\,400$ teenagers by the transportation department of a particular city reveals that teenagers' preference for the type of home-to-school transportation changes with time. The following table shows the results of this study.
From:
Bus Bicycle Electric Scooter
To: Bus $0.2$ $0.2$ $0$
Bicycle $0.4$ $0.4$ $0.4$
Electric Scooter $0.4$ $0.4$ $0.6$
For example, $40%$ of teenagers who used to go to school by bus now go by bicycle. How many teenagers would eventually go to school on electric scooters if the listed probabilities remained constant over many years?
q-141024.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.2 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.6\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix ${P}^{2}$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. 
As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.2 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.8 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.4 & -0.6 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & -0.4\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.8 & 0.2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.4 & -0.6 & 0.4 & 0 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & -0.4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=5{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=5{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=\frac{5}{2}{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{4}{5}{x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}+(\frac{4}{5}{x}_{3})-{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{4}{5}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{x}_{3}+\frac{4}{5}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 2{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10} \\ \frac{4}{10} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, after many years, $\frac{1}{2}$ of the teenagers will go to school in electric scooters. Therefore, the total number of teenagers in the city that will go to school in electric scooters will be

$$
\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\,400=1\,700.
$$
